rte-siege-of-tyre.why: After his victory at Issus, Alexander chose to secure the eastern Mediterranean coast before marching inland, so that the Persian fleet would have no harbours. Tyre offered to submit but refused to let him sacrifice in its island temple of Melqart, and he would not leave a defiant naval base behind him.
rte-siege-of-tyre.impact: Ancient accounts say thousands of Tyrians were killed and many more sold into slavery. Phoenician squadrons deserted the Persian fleet, Gaza fell soon afterwards and Egypt surrendered without a fight. Over the centuries the mole gathered silt and permanently joined the island to the mainland.

rte-death-of-alexander.why: Alexander had returned from India through the Gedrosian desert and was planning new campaigns, reportedly against Arabia. Years of wounds, heavy drinking and the recent death of his close friend Hephaestion had taken their toll. The cause of his fever is still debated, with disease more widely accepted than poison.
rte-death-of-alexander.impact: His half-brother Arrhidaeus and his posthumous son Alexander IV were named joint kings, but both were later murdered. Greek language and city life spread across the Near East under the successor kingdoms, and Alexandria in Egypt grew into the leading centre of Hellenistic learning.

rte-battle-of-carrhae.why: Crassus held Syria as his province under the arrangement with Caesar and Pompey, and wanted military glory to match theirs. Parthia had given Rome no clear cause for war. He ignored the Armenian king's advice to advance through hill country and crossed open plains that suited cavalry.
rte-battle-of-carrhae.impact: Several legionary eagles were captured and thousands of Roman prisoners were taken east. The loss was felt as a humiliation until Augustus negotiated the return of the standards in 20 BC, which he celebrated on coins and monuments. Parthia remained the one neighbouring power that Rome could not simply overawe.

rte-death-of-cleopatra.why: Cleopatra had kept Egypt independent by allying herself first with Julius Caesar and then with Mark Antony, who shared rule of the Roman world with Octavian. Octavian presented the conflict as a foreign war against her, and after Actium her remaining allies and troops deserted.
rte-death-of-cleopatra.impact: Caesarion, her son by Caesar, was killed on Octavian's orders, while her children by Antony were taken to Rome. Egypt's grain and treasure helped Octavian pay his soldiers and feed the capital. The manner of her death, traditionally a snakebite, is uncertain and has fascinated writers and artists ever since.

rte-destruction-of-second-temple.why: Revolt broke out in 66 after years of tension over Roman taxation, heavy-handed governors and religious offence. The rebels drove out the Roman garrison and defeated a relief force. Vespasian reconquered Galilee, then left to claim the imperial throne, leaving his son Titus to finish the war.
rte-destruction-of-second-temple.impact: Without the Temple, sacrifice and the priesthood lost their central place, and Jewish religious life came to centre on the synagogue, prayer and the study of the Torah under the rabbis. Rome diverted the former Temple tax to its own treasury, and many captives were enslaved.

rte-fall-of-nineveh.why: Assyria had been weakened by civil war over the succession after the death of Ashurbanipal and by the strain of holding down a vast empire. Babylon broke away under Nabopolassar in 626 BC. The Medes of western Iran joined him, having already sacked the city of Ashur in 614 BC.
rte-fall-of-nineveh.impact: The Assyrian court retreated west to Harran, which fell soon afterwards, and Assyria vanished as a state. The ruins of Nineveh lay buried until the nineteenth century, when excavators recovered palace reliefs and the clay tablets of Ashurbanipal's library, including the Epic of Gilgamesh.

rte-battle-of-pelusium.why: Cyrus the Great had already conquered Media, Lydia and Babylon, leaving Egypt as the last great independent power in the region. His son Cambyses inherited the plan to take it. The experienced pharaoh Amasis died shortly before the invasion, leaving his newly crowned son to face it.
rte-battle-of-pelusium.impact: Cambyses took the titles of a pharaoh, and Egypt became a wealthy province paying tribute to Persia. Greek writers such as Herodotus painted him as a cruel and impious ruler, though the Egyptian evidence is more mixed. Revolts against Persian rule recurred until Alexander arrived in 332 BC.

rte-burning-of-persepolis.why: Alexander had defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BC and then taken Babylon and Susa. Persepolis was the dynastic heart of the empire and held an enormous royal treasury. His army spent the winter there, and he had the treasure carried away before the fire.
rte-burning-of-persepolis.impact: The captured treasure paid for Alexander's later campaigns and put large quantities of coin into circulation. The site was never restored as a royal capital. The fire also baked and buried clay administrative tablets, which have given modern scholars a detailed record of how the empire was run.

rte-pompey-takes-jerusalem.why: Pompey was in the east after defeating Mithridates of Pontus and had just turned what was left of the Seleucid kingdom into the Roman province of Syria. Two Hasmonean brothers, Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, were fighting over the throne, and both appealed to him for support.
rte-pompey-takes-jerusalem.impact: Pompey confirmed Hyrcanus as high priest but without the title of king, and stripped Judea of the coastal and Greek cities it had conquered. Judea paid tribute to Rome from then on. Aristobulus was taken to Rome as a prisoner and displayed in Pompey's triumph.

rte-death-of-julian.why: Julian, a nephew of Constantine, had been raised a Christian but rejected the faith, and became sole emperor in 361. He inherited a long-running war with Persia. His army reached the capital Ctesiphon but could not take it, and he turned back through hostile country short of supplies.
rte-death-of-julian.impact: The treaty handed over the fortress city of Nisibis, whose inhabitants had to leave, and Rome gave up its influence in Armenia. Julian's religious programme died with him. Every later emperor was Christian, and by the end of the century pagan worship was being banned by law.

rte-siege-of-lachish.why: King Hezekiah of Judah had stopped paying tribute to Assyria after the death of Sargon II, joining a wider revolt encouraged by Egypt. Sennacherib marched west to restore control. Lachish guarded the approach to Jerusalem from the lowlands and was the main fortress in his path.
rte-siege-of-lachish.impact: Many inhabitants were deported, as the reliefs show. Sennacherib went on to blockade Jerusalem but did not take it, and Hezekiah kept his throne by paying a heavy tribute. The campaign is unusual in being described in both Assyrian royal inscriptions and the Hebrew Bible, with different emphases.

rte-battle-of-megiddo-609.why: Assyria was collapsing, and Josiah had used its weakness to assert Judah's independence and extend his influence northwards. Egypt preferred a surviving Assyria as a buffer against Babylon. Josiah's reasons for opposing Necho are not recorded, and the biblical accounts of the encounter differ in detail.
rte-battle-of-megiddo-609.impact: Necho soon deposed Josiah's son Jehoahaz and installed another son, Jehoiakim, as a tribute-paying king. After Babylon beat Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC, Judah changed masters. Later rebellions against Babylon led to the destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple in about 586 BC.

rte-battle-of-raphia.why: The Ptolemies and Seleucids had fought repeatedly over Coele-Syria, covering southern Syria and Palestine, since the division of Alexander's empire. Antiochus III had overrun much of it in the Fourth Syrian War. Ptolemy's ministers stalled with negotiations while they raised and drilled a new army.
rte-battle-of-raphia.impact: Antiochus withdrew and made peace, but returned and took the region for good at the Battle of Panium around 200 BC. In Egypt, native soldiers armed for the campaign grew more assertive, and a long revolt later detached Upper Egypt from Ptolemaic control for about two decades.

rte-battle-of-hormozdgan.why: Parthian kings ruled loosely through regional sub-kings, and the dynasty had been weakened by wars with Rome and by rivalry within the royal family. Ardashir, a local ruler in Persis in the south-west, spent years absorbing his neighbours before challenging the king directly.
rte-battle-of-hormozdgan.impact: Ardashir took the title King of Kings and built a more centralised state than the Parthians had. The Sasanians promoted Zoroastrianism with royal backing and claimed the heritage of ancient Persia. Within a few years they were attacking Roman Mesopotamia, opening centuries of intermittent war.

rte-battle-of-emesa.why: During the crisis of the third century, Rome relied on Odaenathus of Palmyra to defend the east against Persia. After his murder his widow Zenobia ruled for their young son and expanded far beyond that role. Aurelian, having secured the Danube and Italy, marched east to reunite the empire.
rte-battle-of-emesa.impact: Zenobia was taken to Rome and, according to most accounts, displayed in Aurelian's triumph. Palmyra revolted again the following year and was sacked, ending its time as a great caravan city. Aurelian then recovered the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, reuniting the Roman world.

rte-crossing-the-rubicon.why: Caesar's command in Gaul was ending, and his opponents in the Senate demanded that he give up his army and return as a private citizen, which would expose him to prosecution. Compromise talks failed. In January the Senate passed an emergency decree against him, and the tribunes supporting him fled Rome.
rte-crossing-the-rubicon.impact: Pompey and much of the Senate abandoned Rome within weeks, and Caesar took Italy almost without fighting. He went on to win campaigns in Spain, Greece and Africa and was named dictator for life. That concentration of power led to his assassination in 44 BC and to further civil wars.

rte-octavian-becomes-augustus.why: As Julius Caesar's adopted heir, Octavian had defeated Caesar's assassins and then Antony and Cleopatra, leaving him without rivals. Caesar's murder had shown the danger of open monarchy. In January 27 BC he formally handed his powers back to the Senate, which responded by granting him honours and provinces.
rte-octavian-becomes-augustus.impact: The arrangement gave Rome stable one-man rule behind republican forms, and Augustus held power until his death in AD 14. It ended decades of civil war and began the long period of relative peace known as the Pax Romana. The month Sextilis was later renamed August in his honour.

rte-great-fire-of-rome.why: Rome was a crowded city of timber-framed tenements and narrow lanes, and fires were common. This one began among shops full of flammable goods and was driven by wind in the summer heat. According to Tacitus, Nero was at Antium when it started and returned to organise relief.
rte-great-fire-of-rome.impact: Tacitus records that only four of the city's fourteen districts escaped damage. Nero's vast new palace on the cleared land, and the money raised for rebuilding, deepened resentment among the elite. Christian tradition places the deaths of the apostles Peter and Paul in the persecution that followed.

rte-battle-of-the-milvian-bridge.why: Diocletian's system of four co-emperors had broken down into rival claimants. Constantine had been proclaimed by his father's troops at York in 306, while Maxentius held Rome and Italy. In 312 Constantine crossed the Alps and won a string of victories in northern Italy before marching on the capital.
rte-battle-of-the-milvian-bridge.impact: Maxentius drowned in the Tiber during the rout. Constantine disbanded the Praetorian Guard, which had backed his rival. The following year he and his eastern colleague Licinius agreed to tolerate Christianity, and he began funding large churches in Rome, including the Lateran basilica.

rte-visigoths-sack-rome.why: Alaric's Goths had been settled inside the empire and had served in Roman armies, and he wanted land, pay and a senior command. After the general Stilicho was executed in 408, the court at Ravenna refused to negotiate seriously. Alaric besieged Rome three times before his troops finally entered.
rte-visigoths-sack-rome.impact: By ancient standards the sack was restrained, and the main churches were spared. Pagans blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods, prompting Augustine to write The City of God in reply. Alaric died within months, and his people later settled in Gaul and then Spain.

rte-battle-of-chaeronea.why: Philip had turned Macedon from a weak kingdom into the strongest state in the Greek world, with a professional army and rich gold mines. He advanced steadily southwards. The Athenian orator Demosthenes had long warned against him and finally persuaded Thebes, an old rival, to join an alliance.
rte-battle-of-chaeronea.impact: Philip treated Athens leniently but placed a garrison in Thebes. The League of Corinth appointed him to lead a war against Persia, but he was assassinated in 336 BC and the plan passed to Alexander. The Greek city-states never fully recovered their freedom of action in foreign affairs.

rte-battle-of-issus.why: Alexander had crossed into Asia in 334 BC, won at the Granicus and marched through Anatolia. Darius raised a large army and took personal command. The two armies passed each other unknowingly, and Darius ended up behind Alexander on ground too narrow to make use of his numbers.
rte-battle-of-issus.impact: Darius later offered territory and a ransom for his family, which Alexander refused. The Persian baggage captured at Damascus gave him ample funds. Rather than chase Darius inland, he turned south along the coast, which led to the sieges of Tyre and Gaza and the occupation of Egypt.

rte-council-of-nicaea.why: Having defeated Licinius in 324, Constantine ruled the whole empire and wanted a united Church to support it. A dispute begun in Alexandria, where the priest Arius taught that the Son was created by the Father and was not eternal, had spread across the eastern provinces.
rte-council-of-nicaea.impact: The creed described the Son as of one substance with the Father, wording still recited in a later revised form by most Christian churches. The dispute did not end, and Arian views flourished for decades, particularly among the Goths. The council also set a precedent for emperors intervening in doctrine.

rte-constantinople-inaugurated.why: Emperors had long since stopped living in Rome, which was far from the threatened frontiers on the Danube and the Euphrates. After becoming sole ruler in 324, Constantine wanted a base close to both and a city of his own founding. Byzantium had a fine natural harbour and was easy to defend.
rte-constantinople-inaugurated.impact: The city received its own senate and a free grain supply, and drew wealth and talent eastwards. Its position made it a hub of trade between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. Later land walls kept attackers out for centuries, until crusaders took it in 1204 and the Ottomans in 1453.

rte-battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains.why: Attila had built a Hunnic empire north of the Danube and extracted large payments of gold from the eastern Roman court. When those payments stopped, he turned west. He crossed the Rhine in 451 and was besieging Orléans when Aetius, who knew the Huns well, assembled a coalition against him.
rte-battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains.impact: Attila died in 453, and his empire broke up within a few years as subject peoples rebelled. Aetius was killed by the emperor Valentinian III in 454. The battle showed that Rome could now defend Gaul only with the help of the barbarian kingdoms settled inside it.

rte-battle-of-leuctra.why: Sparta had dominated Greece since winning the Peloponnesian War and had even occupied the citadel of Thebes for a time. Thebes expelled the garrison and rebuilt its leadership of Boeotia. At a peace conference in 371 BC Sparta refused to accept this, and sent an army to enforce its will.
rte-battle-of-leuctra.impact: Epaminondas invaded the Peloponnese the following winter and freed Messenia, whose helot population had worked Sparta's land for centuries. That removed the economic basis of Spartan power. Theban dominance lasted only until his death at the Battle of Mantinea in 362 BC.

rte-battle-of-ipsus.why: After Alexander's death his generals divided the empire, and Antigonus came to hold most of its Asian territory. He and his son Demetrius took royal titles in 306 BC and aimed to rule it all. Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus and Ptolemy, each of them threatened, combined against the pair.
rte-battle-of-ipsus.impact: Lysimachus took much of Anatolia and Seleucus gained Syria, where he founded Antioch. Ptolemy, who had not fought, occupied southern Syria, which caused the later Syrian Wars. Demetrius escaped, and his descendants eventually secured Macedon. Seleucus had obtained his elephants by ceding eastern lands to Chandragupta Maurya.

rte-battle-of-cynoscephalae.why: Philip V had allied with Hannibal during Rome's war with Carthage, which the Senate did not forget. Once Carthage was beaten, Pergamon, Rhodes and Athens appealed to Rome against Macedonian aggression in the Aegean. Rome declared war in 200 BC, and Flamininus won over most of the Greek states.
rte-battle-of-cynoscephalae.impact: Philip kept his throne but paid an indemnity, surrendered most of his fleet and withdrew his garrisons from Greece. The Roman army left in 194 BC, but Rome now acted as arbiter of Greek affairs. Its ally the Aetolian League felt cheated and soon invited Antiochus III to intervene.

rte-battle-of-pydna.why: Perseus, son of Philip V, had rebuilt Macedonian strength and courted support among the Greek states, which alarmed Rome and its ally Pergamon. Rome declared war in 171 BC. Its first commanders achieved little, until the experienced Aemilius Paullus took over and manoeuvred Perseus out of a strong defensive position.
rte-battle-of-pydna.impact: Perseus was paraded in Paullus's triumph and died in captivity. Macedon was split into four republics, and Epirus was plundered with huge numbers enslaved. A thousand Achaean hostages went to Italy, among them the historian Polybius. The booty was so great that direct taxation of Roman citizens in Italy was suspended.

rte-death-of-tiberius-gracchus.why: Overseas conquests had enriched Rome's elite, who built large estates worked by slaves, while many small farmers lost their land. Tiberius bypassed the Senate, had a fellow tribune deposed for vetoing his bill, and then sought re-election, which his opponents called a bid for tyranny.
rte-death-of-tiberius-gracchus.impact: His land commission carried on working after his death. Ten years later his brother Gaius pursued wider reforms and also died violently. Politics divided between those who worked through the popular assemblies and those who defended senatorial authority, and force became an accepted way of settling disputes.

rte-saladin-retakes-jerusalem.why: Saladin had spent years uniting Egypt and Syria under his rule, surrounding the crusader states. A truce broke down when Reynald of Châtillon attacked a Muslim caravan. The Kingdom of Jerusalem stripped its castles and towns of men for the field army, so after Hattin few defenders remained.
rte-saladin-retakes-jerusalem.impact: The al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock were restored to Muslim worship, while the Church of the Holy Sepulchre was left standing and reopened to pilgrims. The crusaders held on at Tyre, which became the base for their recovery. Jerusalem was returned by treaty in 1229 and lost again in 1244.

rte-templars-arrested.why: The Templars had been founded to protect pilgrims and defend the crusader states, and grew wealthy through donations and banking. After the fall of Acre in 1291 they had lost their main purpose. Philip had already seized the property of Jews and Italian bankers in his kingdom.
rte-templars-arrested.impact: Pope Clement V suppressed the order at the Council of Vienne in 1312 and assigned most of its property to the Hospitallers, though rulers kept a share. Jacques de Molay was burned in Paris in 1314. The affair showed how much pressure the French crown could put on the papacy.

rte-joan-of-arc-burned.why: Joan, a peasant girl from Domrémy, said that the voices of saints told her to drive the English from France. The English needed to discredit her, since her successes implied divine backing for Charles VII. The court was led by Bishop Pierre Cauchon, a supporter of the English cause.
rte-joan-of-arc-burned.impact: Her death did not revive English fortunes. Burgundy made peace with Charles VII in 1435, Paris was recovered the following year, and the English were gradually pushed out of France. The verdict was annulled in 1456. She was canonised in 1920 and became a national symbol of France.

rte-fall-of-acre.why: The Mamluks, who ruled Egypt and Syria, had been taking crusader castles and towns one by one since the 1260s, and Tripoli fell in 1289. Europe sent little help. A massacre of Muslim merchants in Acre by newly arrived Italian crusaders in 1290 gave the sultan grounds to end a truce.
rte-fall-of-acre.impact: The Mamluks demolished coastal fortifications so that no crusade could use them as a landing point. The Hospitallers moved to Cyprus and later Rhodes, and Cyprus became the main Latin outpost in the east. Plans for a new crusade continued for generations, but none recovered the Holy Land.

rte-black-prince-poitiers.why: Edward III claimed the French throne through his mother, and war had resumed after the Black Death. English strategy relied on the chevauchée, a destructive mounted raid meant to ruin French revenues and provoke battle. The prince, heading back to Gascony laden with plunder, was overtaken by King John's larger army.
rte-black-prince-poitiers.impact: France was left to the young dauphin, who faced a revolt in Paris and the peasant rising known as the Jacquerie. The Treaty of Brétigny in 1360 set John's ransom at three million gold crowns and gave Edward an enlarged Aquitaine. John died in London in 1364 with the ransom unpaid in full.

rte-las-navas-de-tolosa.why: The Almohads, a Berber dynasty from Morocco, had beaten Castile heavily at Alarcos in 1195. Alfonso VIII of Castile sought revenge, and Pope Innocent III declared a crusade to support him. Kings who were often rivals agreed to fight together, though most of the foreign crusaders left before the battle.
rte-las-navas-de-tolosa.impact: Almohad rule in Iberia fragmented into small kingdoms over the following decades. Aragon took Valencia in 1238, and Portugal completed its advance to the Algarve. By the middle of the century only the emirate of Granada remained under Muslim rule, surviving as a tributary of Castile until 1492.

rte-battle-on-the-ice.why: German and Danish crusaders had conquered the pagan peoples of the eastern Baltic and now pressed against Orthodox Novgorod, at a time when the Mongols had just devastated the other Rus principalities. The knights had seized Pskov. Alexander, who had beaten the Swedes on the Neva in 1240, was recalled to lead the defence.
rte-battle-on-the-ice.impact: The scale of the battle is disputed, and it was probably smaller than legend suggests. A peace settled the border, which stayed roughly along the Narva river and Lake Peipus. Alexander chose to submit to the Mongols while resisting the Catholic west. He was later made an Orthodox saint.

rte-battle-of-castillon.why: Charles VII had reformed French finances and created a standing army with a powerful artillery train organised by the Bureau brothers. The French took Gascony in 1451, but Bordeaux, long tied to England by the wine trade, invited the English back. Talbot retook the city in 1452.
rte-battle-of-castillon.impact: No treaty ended the war, and English monarchs kept the title King of France until 1801. Defeat discredited Henry VI's government and contributed to the Wars of the Roses, which broke out in 1455. The battle is often cited as an early field victory decided largely by gunpowder weapons.

rte-barbarossa-drowns.why: Frederick had ruled Germany for nearly four decades and had gone on the Second Crusade as a young man. After Jerusalem fell in 1187 he took the cross and chose the overland route through Hungary and Byzantium. His army had just fought its way across Anatolia and taken the Seljuk capital, Iconium.
rte-barbarossa-drowns.impact: His son Frederick of Swabia led the remnant to Acre, where he died of disease. Germans at that siege founded a field hospital that developed into the Teutonic Order. In German legend the emperor never died but sleeps beneath the Kyffhäuser mountain until his country needs him.

rte-battle-of-sluys.why: Edward III had claimed the French crown and needed to ship an army to his allies in Flanders. France had gathered a large fleet, including hired Genoese galleys, to stop him, and had been raiding English ports such as Southampton. Its commanders chose to wait in the anchorage.
rte-battle-of-sluys.impact: The victory ended the threat of a French invasion for some years and let English armies cross the Channel freely. It brought Edward little immediate gain on land, since his siege of Tournai failed and he ran out of money. French losses in men were very heavy, though estimates vary.

rte-battle-of-arsuf.why: Acre had surrendered to the crusaders in July 1191 after a two-year siege. Philip II then went home, leaving Richard in command. Richard needed a port close to Jerusalem and marched along the shore so that his fleet could supply him. Saladin shadowed the column, trying to provoke it into breaking formation.
rte-battle-of-arsuf.impact: Saladin avoided further pitched battles and had the walls of Ascalon demolished to deny it to the crusaders. Richard twice advanced towards Jerusalem and judged he could not hold it. The Treaty of Jaffa in 1192 left the coast to the crusaders and allowed Christian pilgrims to visit the city.

rte-battle-of-montgisard.why: Saladin had ruled Egypt since 1169 and had recently added Damascus, giving him territory on two sides of the kingdom. Much of the crusader army was away campaigning in northern Syria with the Count of Flanders. Saladin let his troops disperse to raid and forage, expecting no resistance.
rte-battle-of-montgisard.impact: Saladin escaped back to Egypt with heavy losses, and the kingdom gained a few years of breathing space. He returned to win at Marj Ayyun and destroy the new castle at Jacob's Ford in 1179. Baldwin died in 1185, and the succession quarrels that followed weakened the kingdom before Hattin.

rte-siege-of-lisbon.why: Afonso had only recently begun ruling Portugal as a king and was pushing his frontier south towards the Tagus. He had taken Santarém that spring. The crusaders' fleet put in at Porto, where the bishop urged them to help, and Afonso promised them the plunder of the city.
rte-siege-of-lisbon.impact: It was one of the few lasting successes of the Second Crusade, whose main armies failed in Anatolia and at Damascus. An English priest, Gilbert of Hastings, became bishop of Lisbon, and some crusaders settled there. Control of the Tagus estuary gave Portugal a secure base for expanding further south.

rte-krak-des-chevaliers-falls.why: The Hospitallers had held the castle since 1142 and used it to dominate the gap between the coast and the Syrian interior. By 1271 the order was short of men and money. Baibars had already taken Antioch in 1268 and was picking off the remaining inland strongholds one at a time.
rte-krak-des-chevaliers-falls.impact: The garrison was allowed to leave for Tripoli. Baibars repaired the castle, turned its chapel into a mosque and used it as a Mamluk base against the remaining crusader coast. It survives as one of the best preserved medieval castles and is a World Heritage Site, though damaged in the Syrian civil war.

rte-battle-of-nicopolis.why: The Ottomans had expanded rapidly in the Balkans after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 and now threatened Hungary and blockaded Constantinople. A truce in the Hundred Years' War freed French and Burgundian knights to answer the call for a crusade, led by the son of the Duke of Burgundy.
rte-battle-of-nicopolis.impact: Bayezid had many prisoners killed and held the leading nobles for a large ransom. The last independent Bulgarian territory was absorbed. Constantinople was reprieved only because Timur defeated and captured Bayezid at Ankara in 1402. Western rulers made no comparable effort until the Crusade of Varna in 1444.

rte-tang-dynasty-founded.why: The Sui had reunified China in 589 after centuries of division, but exhausted it with vast projects such as the Grand Canal and failed invasions of the Korean kingdom of Goguryeo. Rebellions spread across the country. Li Yuan, a northern aristocrat and garrison commander, seized the capital in 617.
rte-tang-dynasty-founded.impact: The Tang built on Sui law codes and civil service examinations and extended Chinese control deep into Central Asia. Poetry, painting and Buddhism flourished, and Japan and Korea borrowed Tang institutions. The dynasty lasted until 907, though it never fully recovered from the An Lushan rebellion of the 750s.

rte-song-dynasty-founded.why: After the Tang fell in 907, northern China passed through five short-lived dynasties, each founded by a military strongman, while the south split into separate kingdoms. The Later Zhou throne had just passed to a child. Zhao, sent out to meet a reported invasion, was acclaimed by his officers at Chenqiao.
rte-song-dynasty-founded.impact: Taizu persuaded his generals to retire and placed the army under civil officials chosen by examination, ending the cycle of coups. The price was military weakness against northern neighbours. The Song lost north China to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and ruled from Hangzhou until the Mongol conquest.

rte-ming-dynasty-founded.why: Mongol rule had been undermined by disputes over the succession, inflation from overprinted paper money, epidemics and disastrous Yellow River floods. Resentment fed rebel movements along the Yangtze. Zhu, orphaned by famine as a youth, outlasted rival warlords and defeated Chen Youliang at Lake Poyang in 1363.
rte-ming-dynasty-founded.impact: The Hongwu Emperor abolished the post of chancellor and concentrated power in his own hands, purging officials he distrusted. His dynasty ruled until 1644. Under his son the Yongle Emperor the capital moved to Beijing, the Forbidden City was built, and Zheng He's fleets sailed across the Indian Ocean.

rte-death-of-genghis-khan.why: Born Temüjin, probably around 1162, he united the Mongol tribes and took the title Genghis Khan in 1206. He then attacked northern China and destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia. The Western Xia had failed to send troops for that campaign, so he returned to punish them. The cause of his death is unknown.
rte-death-of-genghis-khan.impact: He had named his third son Ögedei as successor, a choice confirmed by an assembly in 1229. The Western Xia state was destroyed. His laws and his habit of promoting on merit helped hold the empire together for a time, but by the 1260s it had divided into four khanates.

rte-kamikaze-destroys-mongol-fleet.why: Kublai had demanded that Japan submit as a tributary, and the Kamakura shogunate refused. A first invasion in 1274 withdrew after brief fighting. Japan then executed Mongol envoys and built a stone wall along Hakata Bay. Having conquered the Southern Song in 1279, Kublai could use its ships and sailors.
rte-kamikaze-destroys-mongol-fleet.impact: Japan remained unconquered, but the shogunate had no captured land to reward its warriors and had to keep costly defences ready for years, which weakened it before its fall in 1333. Divers have found wrecks from the fleet off Takashima. The word kamikaze was revived in the Second World War.

rte-yuan-dynasty-proclaimed.why: Kublai had become Great Khan in 1260 after a civil war with his brother Ariq Böke, but the western khanates barely recognised him. His power base was northern China, and Chinese advisers urged him to rule in a familiar form to win over officials and subjects. The name came from the Book of Changes.
rte-yuan-dynasty-proclaimed.impact: Kublai completed the conquest of the Southern Song in 1279, uniting north and south China for the first time in centuries. Mongols and Central Asians were favoured over Chinese for high office. Paper money circulated widely and the Grand Canal was extended to supply the capital. The dynasty lasted until 1368.

rte-battle-of-legnica.why: After conquering the Rus principalities, the Mongols turned on Hungary, partly because its king had sheltered Cuman refugees. The force sent into Poland was meant to stop Polish and Bohemian rulers helping the Hungarians. It had already burned Kraków before meeting Henry, who was waiting for a Bohemian army.
rte-battle-of-legnica.impact: Two days later the main Mongol army destroyed the Hungarians at Mohi. The Mongols withdrew from Central Europe in 1242, a retreat usually linked to the death of the Great Khan Ögedei, though historians debate the reasons. Henry's death split Silesia among his heirs and ended his family's hopes of reuniting Poland.

rte-diamond-sutra-printed.why: Woodblock printing had developed in China by about the eighth century, building on the earlier invention of paper and the use of carved seals and stone rubbings. Buddhists valued copying scriptures as a way of earning merit, and printing allowed many copies. The colophon says Wang Jie made it on behalf of his parents.
rte-diamond-sutra-printed.impact: The scroll's skilled illustration shows that printing was already a mature craft by 868. Printing spread through East Asia and under the Song was used for classics, calendars and paper money. The cave library where it was found held tens of thousands of manuscripts, now divided among collections in several countries.

rte-timur-sacks-delhi.why: The Delhi Sultanate had been breaking apart since the death of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in 1388, with rival claimants and provinces going their own way. Timur had already conquered Persia and much of Central Asia. He justified the invasion as punishing rulers too tolerant of their Hindu subjects, though plunder was a clear motive.
rte-timur-sacks-delhi.impact: Contemporary accounts describe mass killing of prisoners and townspeople, though the numbers are uncertain. Delhi took generations to recover, and the Tughlaq dynasty ended in 1413. Regional sultanates such as Gujarat and Jaunpur went their own way. Timur's descendant Babur later invoked the conquest when founding the Mughal Empire in 1526.

rte-mongol-siege-of-kyiv.why: Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, led the western campaign approved by the Great Khan Ögedei in 1235, with Subutai as chief general. The Rus princes were divided and fought each other for control of Kyiv itself. The north-eastern cities had fallen in 1237 and 1238, and Chernihiv in 1239.
rte-mongol-siege-of-kyiv.impact: A papal envoy passing through six years later described a city reduced to about two hundred houses. Political leadership among the Rus shifted to the north-east, eventually to Moscow, and to Galicia-Volhynia in the west. Much of the Kyiv region later came under Lithuanian rule.

rte-battle-of-yamen.why: The Mongols had been at war with the Southern Song since 1235. The long siege of Xiangyang, which fell in 1273, opened the Yangtze, and the Song capital Hangzhou surrendered in 1276. Loyalists carried two young princes south by sea and crowned each in turn as they retreated.
rte-battle-of-yamen.impact: It was the first time all of China had been ruled by a non-Chinese dynasty. Song loyalists such as Wen Tianxiang, who refused to serve the Yuan and was executed, became models of fidelity for later generations. Southern ports like Quanzhou kept trading under the Mongols and prospered.

rte-battle-of-the-kalka.why: Subutai and Jebe had been sent west to hunt the fleeing shah of Khwarazm, and after his death were allowed to continue exploring. They crossed the Caucasus and defeated the Cumans, whose khan appealed to his son-in-law, a Rus prince. The Rus killed Mongol envoys before marching out.
rte-battle-of-the-kalka.impact: The Mongols rode back east, and the Rus princes, unsure who the invaders were, made no preparations for their return. Subutai came back in 1237 with a far larger army and first-hand knowledge of the country. The Cumans were scattered, and many later fled into Hungary.

rte-battle-of-chioggia.why: Venice and Genoa had fought three earlier wars over trading posts in the Aegean and Black Sea. This one began over the island of Tenedos, which controls the approach to the Dardanelles. Genoa was allied with Hungary and Padua, so Venice was pressed by land and sea at once.
rte-battle-of-chioggia.impact: The Peace of Turin in 1381 was not especially favourable to Venice on paper, but Genoa was financially exhausted and fell into internal strife, at times accepting foreign rule. Venice recovered quickly and dominated trade with the eastern Mediterranean for the next century.

rte-battle-of-the-zab.why: Many Muslims resented the Umayyads, particularly non-Arab converts who were treated as second-class and supporters of the Prophet's family. The Abbasids, descended from the Prophet's uncle, organised a secret movement in Khurasan. Open revolt began there in 747 under Abu Muslim, when the dynasty was already weakened by civil war.
rte-battle-of-the-zab.impact: Marwan was hunted down and killed in Egypt, and most of the Umayyad family was massacred. One prince, Abd al-Rahman, escaped to Spain and founded an independent emirate at Córdoba. Persian officials and customs gained influence at the new court, and the caliphate became less exclusively Arab.

rte-treaty-of-stralsund.why: Valdemar IV had rebuilt Danish royal power and in 1361 sacked Visby on Gotland, a major Hanseatic trading town. He also threatened the herring markets of Scania and the tolls on the Sound. The towns formed the Confederation of Cologne in 1367, found allies including Sweden, and attacked Denmark's coasts.
rte-treaty-of-stralsund.impact: The castles came with a large share of their revenues for fifteen years. The League also won a say in the choice of the next Danish king. Its dominance faded in the following century as the Kalmar Union united the Scandinavian crowns and Dutch shippers entered the Baltic.
